q: 1. The instrument generally used to measure the depth of foundation is ..........
explain: Boning rods are used in sets (usually three) to check levels and maintain a uniform depth or gradient in foundation trenches.

q: 2. The foundation in which a cantilever beam is provided to join two footings, is known as
explain: A strap footing uses a connecting beam (strap) to distribute loads between an eccentrically loaded footing and an interior one.

q: 3. The piles driven to increase the capacity of supporting loads on vertical piles are known as ........
explain: Raking piles are driven at an angle (inclined) to the vertical to resist horizontal thrust or increase lateral stability.

q: 4. Black cotton soil is unsuitable for foundations because its
options: property to undergo a volumetric change due to variation of moisture content
explain: Black cotton soil swells significantly when wet and shrinks when dry, which can cause foundation failure.

q: 5. The lower part of a structure which transmits the load to the soil is known as ..........
explain: The foundation is the lowest part of a building that receives the total load and distributes it safely over a large area of soil.

q: 6. The foundation in a building is provide to ..........
options: distribute the load over a large area
increase the overall stability of the structure
transmit the load to the bearing surface at uniform rate
explain: Foundations serve multiple purposes: load distribution, providing a level surface, and ensuring the stability of the entire building.

q: 7. The minimum load which causes the failure of a foundation is called ............ of the soil.
explain: Ultimate bearing strength is the maximum gross pressure at the base of the foundation at which the soil fails in shear.

q: 8. The safe bearing capacity of a soil is given by ..........
options: ultimate bearing strength / factor of safety
nominal strength x factor of safety
ultimate bearing strength x factor of safety
explain: Safe bearing capacity is calculated by dividing the ultimate bearing capacity by a Factor of Safety (usually 2 to 3).

q: 9. For the buildings on clayey soils, the minimum depth of foundation is ..........
explain: In clayey soils, foundations must be deeper to avoid the zone of seasonal moisture variation; typically 0.9m to 1.6m is required.

q: 10. The weight of the furniture stored in a building is termed as ..........
explain: Live loads (or imposed loads) include the weight of movable objects like furniture, occupants, and stored goods that are not a permanent part of the structure.

q: 11. The size of the plate used in plate loading test in clayey soils is ..........
explain: For cohesive (clayey) soils, a larger plate size of 60 cm x 60 cm is preferred to capture the settlement behavior accurately.

q: 12. The size of the plate used in plate loading test in gravelly or sandy soils is ..........
explain: For non-cohesive (sandy or gravelly) soils, a standard smaller plate of 30 cm x 30 cm is often utilized.

q: 13. Columns in a workshop supporting Gantry Cranes will have ..........
explain: Grillage foundations are ideal for heavy isolated column loads in industrial buildings where a large bearing area is required to prevent settlement.

q: 14. The angle of repose for dry sand may be taken as ..........
explain: The angle of repose (internal friction) for dry, loose sand is typically around 30 degrees.

q: 15. The lowest part of a structure which transmits the load to the soil is known as ..........
explain: The foundation is the sub-structure that transfers the building weight to the underlying soil or rock.

q: 16. The foundation in a building is provided to ..........
options: distribute the load over a large area
increase overall stability of the structure
transmit load to the bearing surface(sub soil) at a uniform rate
explain: Foundations ensure stability, prevent unequal settlement, and distribute heavy loads over a wider area to avoid soil failure.

q: 17. The ability of sub-soil to support the load of the structure without yielding is known as ..........
explain: Bearing capacity (or value/power) refers to the soil's resistance to compression and shear failure under structural loads.

q: 18. The maximum bearing capacity of soil is that of ..........
explain: Igneous and hard rocks have the highest safe bearing capacity, often exceeding 3000-4000 kN/m².

q: 19. When the walls are subjected to heavy loading and the bearing capacity of the soil is very low, the wall is constructed on ..........
explain: R.C.C. footings are used for heavy loads on weak soil because reinforcement allows the footing to resist tension and distribute weight more effectively.

q: 20. When heavy structural loads from columns are required to be transferred to a soil of low bearing capacity, the most economical foundation is ..........
explain: Grillage foundations (using steel beams or timber) are economical for spreading heavy column loads over a wide area without deep excavation.

q: 21. In order to protect the beam against corrosion, a minimum cover of ........ is kept on the outer sides of the external beams as well as above the upper flange of the top tier.
explain: In grillage foundations, steel beams are encased in concrete with at least 100 mm cover to protect against moisture and corrosion.

q: 22. In masonry construction, excessive tension is not permissible and hence in order that the supporting area is fully in compression, the width of footing is so adopted that the centre of gravity of the load falls ..........
options: within the middle third of base
within the middle fifth of base
explain: To avoid tension at the base of a masonry footing, the eccentricity of the load must be limited so the resultant force stays within the middle third.

q: 23. In made-up ground having a low value of its bearing power, heavy concentrated structural loads are generally supported by providing ..........
explain: Raft (mat) foundations are best for 'made-up' or soft ground as they bridge over weak spots and prevent differential settlement.

q: 24. Which of the following foundation is used for weaker soil?
explain: While all spread footings help, raft foundations are specifically designed to handle the most challenging weak soil conditions.

q: 25. The raft foundations are generally used when the required area of footing is ........ the total area of the surface.
explain: Standard practice dictates that if the total area of individual footings exceeds 50% (one-half) of the building area, a raft is used.

q: 26. When two or more footings are connected by a beam, it is called ..........
explain: A strap footing consists of two isolated footings joined by a structural 'strap' beam to transfer eccentric loads.

q: 27. A black cotton soil is unsuitable for foundations because it ..........
options: undergoes volumetric changes with the change of atmospheric conditions
explain: Black cotton soil contains montmorillonite clay which expands and contracts violently with moisture changes, causing structures to crack.

q: 28. When the heavy structure is to be constructed in sandy soil, the foundation used is ..........
explain: Depending on the density and depth of the sand, piers, straps, or rafts may be used to provide adequate bearing.

q: 29. Pile foundation is generally used when the soil is ..........
explain: Piles are deep foundations used when surface soil is weak, water-logged, or unreliable, transferring loads to deeper, firmer strata.

q: 30. The type of foundation most suitable for bridges is ..........
explain: Pier foundations are commonly used for bridge structures to transfer heavy loads through water or soft soil to hard rock.

q: 31. A combined footing is commonly used ..........
options: when two columns are spaced close to each other
when two columns are spaced far apart
explain: When columns are so close that their individual footings would overlap, they are merged into a single combined footing.

q: 32. The piles which do not support the load by themselves, but act as a medium to transmit the load from the foundation to the resisting sub-stratum, are known as ..........
explain: End-bearing piles act like columns, transmitting the load through their tips directly to a hard-resisting layer.

q: 33. The piles which are driven in the type of soil whose strength does not increase with depth or where the rate of increase in strength with depth is very slow, are known as ..........
explain: Friction piles derive their carrying capacity from the skin friction between the pile surface and the surrounding soil along the entire length of the pile.

q: 34. In combined footing ..........
options: center of gravity of the column loads must coincide with the center of gravity of the footing
explain: For uniform pressure distribution in a combined footing, the geometric center (C.G.) of the footing must coincide with the resultant C.G. of the loads from both columns.

q: 35. Batter piles are ..........
options: used to function as retaining walls
used to protect concrete deck or other water front structures from the abrasion or impact
driven at an inclination to resist large horizontal inclined forces
driven in granular soil with the aim of increasing the bearing capacity of the soil
explain: Batter piles (or raking piles) are driven at an angle to the vertical to resist lateral loads, such as wind or water pressure.

q: 36. Fender piles are ..........
options: used to function as retaining walls
used to protect concrete deck or other water front structures from the abrasion or impact
driven at an inclination to resist large horizontal inclined forces
driven in granular soil with the aim of increasing the bearing capacity of the soil
explain: Fender piles are provided in waterfront structures to absorb the impact of berthing ships and protect the main structure from damage.

q: 37. Cast-in-situ piles is ..........
options: are cast in position inside the ground
need not be reinforced in ordinary cases
are not subjected to handling or driving stresses
explain: Since they are formed in the ground, cast-in-situ piles avoid the stresses of transport and driving, allowing for more flexible design.

q: 38. A type of cast-in-situ pile suited for places where the ground is soft and offers little resistance to the flow of concrete, is ..........
explain: Vibro-piles use a vibrating casing that compacts the soil and ensures a dense concrete column even in soft soil conditions.

q: 39. A type of cast-in-situ pile which has an enlarged base and a corrugated stem, is ..........
explain: Franki piles feature a 'mushroom' base formed by ramming dry concrete into the soil, significantly increasing the end-bearing area.

q: 40. The diameter of the drilled piles should not exceed ..........
explain: Standard drilled or bored piles for smaller structures typically range up to 600 mm in diameter.

options: cannot withstand large impact stress developed during hand driving
explain: H-piles (steel I-beams) are actually easy to store, handle, and can withstand extremely high driving stresses, making all the provided negative statements false.

q: 42. A steel pile which function more efficiently in soft clay or loose sand, is ..........
explain: The large helical blades of a screw pile provide significant uplift and bearing resistance in soft or loose soils.

q: 43. A screw pile consists of cast iron or steel shaft of external diameter varying from ..........
explain: The central shaft of a screw pile is typically between 150 mm and 300 mm, though the helix blade diameter is much larger.

q: 44. Sheet piles are made of ..........
explain: Sheet piles can be made of timber for light work, reinforced concrete for permanent structures, or steel for high-strength temporary or permanent shoring.

q: 45. When the pile is required to penetrate beds of hard soil or soft rock to reach its required depth, the best method of driving the pile is by ..........
explain: Boring (pre-drilling) removes the hard material that a standard hammer cannot penetrate, allowing the pile to reach the design depth.

q: 46. When the pile is driven by means of water jets, water is forced through the jet pipe under a pressure of ..........
explain: Jetting uses water pressure (0.7 to 1.75 MPa) to displace soil at the pile tip, facilitating easier penetration in sandy or gravelly soils.

q: 47. A watertight structure constructed in connection with excavations for foundations of bridges, piers etc., is known as ..........
explain: A caisson is a permanent, watertight retaining structure used for foundations of bridges and other heavy structures in water or wet ground.

q: 48. In order that the wall may be stable, the lowermost course of the wall footing is made ........ the width of the wall.
explain: According to the rule of thumb for spread footings, the width of the base of the foundation should be twice the width of the wall.

q: 49. The arrangement of supports provided underneath the existing structure without disturbing its stability, is known as ..........
explain: Underpinning is the process of strengthening or deepening the foundation of an existing structure.

q: 50. A raking shore is a system of ..........
options: giving temporary lateral support to an unsafe wall
providing temporary support to the party walls of two buildings where the intermediate building is to be pulled down and rebuilt
providing vertical support to walls and roofs, floors etc. when the lower part of a wall has to be removed for the purpose of providing an opening in the wall
explain: Raking shores consist of inclined timber members (rakers) used to provide lateral support to walls that are bulging or out of plumb.
